questions.stem: In an X-ray tube, how are the X-rays produced?
options: Light from a lamp falls on a metal target and releases X-ray photons
A radioactive source inside the tube emits X-rays when it is switched on
Electrons from a hot filament are accelerated by a high voltage into a metal target
A metal target is heated by a filament until it glows and emits X-rays
questions.explanation: A heated filament, the cathode, releases electrons by thermionic emission. A potential difference of tens of kilovolts accelerates them across the evacuated tube, and when they strike the target, the anode, some of their kinetic energy becomes X-ray photons.

questions.stem: Why is the inside of an X-ray tube a vacuum?
options: So the electrons reach the target without colliding with gas molecules
So the X-rays can travel faster than they would through air
So the filament can be heated without needing an electric current
So the target metal cannot become charged as electrons arrive
questions.explanation: Gas molecules would scatter the electrons and absorb their energy before they reached the target. In a vacuum the electrons gain the full energy eV from the accelerating voltage.

questions.stem: Why is the target in an X-ray tube usually made of tungsten, often with oil cooling or a rotating anode?
options: Tungsten absorbs most of the X-rays produced, so it must be cooled as it absorbs them
The X-rays heat the target as they leave it, so it would melt if not cooled
Tungsten is radioactive and gets hot as it decays, so it must be cooled constantly
Only about 1% of the electrons' energy becomes X-rays, and the rest heats the target
questions.explanation: Most of the electrons' kinetic energy becomes thermal energy in the target, and only a small fraction becomes X-rays. Tungsten has a very high melting point, and cooling or rotating the anode spreads and removes the heat.

questions.stem: What produces the continuous part of an X-ray spectrum?
options: Electrons in the target atoms falling from outer shells into gaps in the n = 1 shell
Nuclei in the target decaying and emitting gamma rays of many different energies
Electrons in the filament being heated to very high temperatures before they leave
Electrons slowing down by different amounts as they pass near nuclei in the target
questions.explanation: An electron decelerated by the field of a nucleus emits a photon carrying the energy it loses. Electrons lose any amount up to their full kinetic energy, so photons of every energy up to a maximum are produced. Transitions between shells give the characteristic lines instead.

questions.stem: How are characteristic X-rays produced in the target of an X-ray tube?
options: An incoming electron is captured by a nucleus, which then emits a high-energy photon
An incoming electron excites an outer electron, which then falls back to its own level
An incoming electron knocks out an inner electron, and an outer electron falls into the gap
An incoming electron is slowed by a nucleus and loses some of its kinetic energy
questions.explanation: When a fast electron ejects an electron from an inner shell, an electron from a higher level drops into the vacancy and emits a photon equal to the energy difference. These differences are large for heavy atoms, giving X-ray photons at fixed energies.

questions.stem: In an X-ray spectrum, what is the difference between K lines and L lines?
options: K lines come from the filament metal; L lines come from the target metal
K lines come from transitions ending on n = 1; L lines from transitions ending on n = 2
K lines come from transitions ending on n = 2; L lines from transitions ending on n = 1
K lines come from slowing electrons; L lines come from transitions between levels
questions.explanation: Characteristic lines are named after the shell where the vacancy is filled: K for n = 1 and L for n = 2. Because the n = 1 level lies much deeper, K-line photons have more energy than L-line photons from the same element.

questions.stem: Two X-ray tubes run at the same voltage, one with a tungsten target and one with a molybdenum target. How do their spectra differ?
options: Their characteristic lines and maximum photon energies both depend on the target metal
Their characteristic lines are at different energies, but their maximum photon energy is the same
Their characteristic lines are at the same energies, but their maximum photon energy differs
Their characteristic lines and maximum photon energies are both exactly the same
questions.explanation: Characteristic lines depend on the energy levels of the target element, so they identify it. The maximum photon energy depends only on the energy the electrons gain, eV, which is the same for the same voltage.

questions.stem: An X-ray spectrum is plotted as intensity against wavelength. Which description fits it?
options: A set of sharp peaks only, with no radiation between them at all
A smooth curve starting at zero wavelength and rising without any peaks
A smooth curve with a single dip at the wavelength of each characteristic line
A smooth curve starting at a minimum wavelength, with sharp peaks on top of it
questions.explanation: The continuous radiation forms a smooth curve that begins at a sharp cut-off, the minimum wavelength set by the tube voltage. The characteristic lines appear as narrow spikes on top. There are no photons shorter than the cut-off.

questions.stem: An X-ray tube operates at 40 kV. What is the greatest energy an X-ray photon from the tube can have?
options: 40 eV
20 keV
80 keV
40 keV
questions.explanation: Each electron gains kinetic energy eV = 40 keV crossing the tube. The most energetic photon is made when an electron loses all of this in a single interaction, so hf(max) = eV = 40 keV.

questions.stem: An X-ray tube operates at 30 kV. What is the maximum frequency of the X-rays it produces? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
questions.explanation: hf(max) = eV, so f(max) = eV/h = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 3.0 × 10⁴)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 7.24 × 10¹⁸ Hz. Using 30 V instead of 30 kV gives 7.24 × 10¹⁵ Hz.

questions.stem: What is the minimum wavelength of X-rays from a tube operating at 25 kV? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The shortest wavelength belongs to the most energetic photon: eV = hc/λ(min), so λ(min) = hc/eV = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸)/(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.5 × 10⁴) = 4.97 × 10⁻¹¹ m.

questions.stem: What is the smallest accelerating voltage an X-ray tube needs to produce photons of wavelength 0.10 nm? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
options: 12 kV
1.2 kV
120 kV
questions.explanation: The photon energy is hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸)/(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.99 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. The electrons need at least this much, so V = E/e = 1.99 × 10⁻¹⁵/1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.2 × 10⁴ V, about 12 kV.

questions.stem: The current through an X-ray tube is doubled while the accelerating voltage stays the same. What happens to the X-rays?
options: Their intensity increases, but the maximum frequency stays the same
Their maximum frequency doubles, but the intensity stays the same
Their intensity and maximum frequency both double
Their maximum frequency halves, because the electrons share the energy
questions.explanation: A larger current means more electrons strike the target each second, so more photons are produced. Each electron still gains only eV, so the maximum photon frequency, eV/h, does not change.

questions.stem: The accelerating voltage of an X-ray tube is increased, with the current unchanged. Which changes occur in the spectrum?
options: The cut-off wavelength gets shorter, and the characteristic lines stay at the same wavelengths
The cut-off wavelength gets longer, and the characteristic lines move to shorter wavelengths
The cut-off wavelength stays the same, and the characteristic lines move to shorter wavelengths
The cut-off wavelength gets shorter, and the characteristic lines move by the same amount
questions.explanation: A higher voltage gives the electrons more energy, so λ(min) = hc/eV decreases and the curve extends to shorter wavelengths. The characteristic lines are fixed by the target's energy levels, so they do not move.

questions.stem: In a target metal, the n = 1 level is at −9.0 keV and the n = 2 level is at −1.0 keV. What is the energy of its K line from n = 2 to n = 1, and the least tube voltage needed to produce it?
options: 9.0 keV, with at least 1.0 kV across the tube
8.0 keV, with at least 9.0 kV across the tube
8.0 keV, with at least 8.0 kV across the tube
10 keV, with at least 10 kV across the tube
questions.explanation: The photon energy is the difference between the levels: 9.0 − 1.0 = 8.0 keV. But first an n = 1 electron must be removed entirely, which needs 9.0 keV, so the electrons must be accelerated through at least 9.0 kV.

questions.stem: A target metal emits a K line with photon energy 8.0 keV. What is its wavelength? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: E = 8.0 × 10³ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, so λ = hc/E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸)/(1.28 × 10⁻¹⁵) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Leaving out the factor of 10³ for keV gives 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ m, an ultraviolet wavelength.

questions.stem: Why does the continuous X-ray spectrum from a tube stop sharply at a minimum wavelength?
options: No electron can give a photon more energy than the eV it gained from the voltage
Shorter wavelengths are all absorbed by the glass walls of the X-ray tube
The target atoms have no energy levels that could produce shorter wavelengths
Shorter wavelengths would need the filament to be heated to a higher temperature
questions.explanation: An electron reaching the target has kinetic energy eV, and at most it converts all of this into one photon. The highest photon energy therefore corresponds to the shortest wavelength, hc/eV. The continuous radiation does not come from energy levels, so their spacing does not set the cut-off.

questions.stem: What is the momentum of an X-ray photon with an energy of 50 keV? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
options: 2.7 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹
2.4 × 10⁻⁶ kg m s⁻¹
1.7 × 10⁻⁴ kg m s⁻¹
8.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: E = 50 × 10³ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, and p = E/c = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁵/3.00 × 10⁸ = 2.7 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹. 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ is the energy in joules, not the momentum.

questions.stem: What happens in Compton scattering?
options: An X-ray photon passes near a nucleus and splits into an electron and a positron
An X-ray photon reflects off a crystal and produces an interference pattern on a screen
An X-ray photon collides with an electron, which recoils, and the photon scatters with a longer wavelength
An X-ray photon is absorbed completely by an electron, which is then ejected from a metal surface
questions.explanation: Compton fired X-rays at a target with loosely bound electrons. The scattered X-rays had longer wavelengths, which he explained as a collision between a photon and an electron. Complete absorption with electron emission is the photoelectric effect.

questions.stem: In Compton scattering, why does the scattered X-ray have a longer wavelength than the incident X-ray?
options: The photon gives some of its energy and momentum to the electron, so its frequency falls
The photon slows down after the collision, so its wavelength must increase to match
The photon gains energy from the moving electron, so its wavelength gets longer
The photon is absorbed and re-emitted by a nucleus, which lowers its energy
questions.explanation: The recoiling electron gains kinetic energy, so the photon loses energy. E = hf, so its frequency falls, and λ = h/p, so its wavelength rises. The scattered photon still travels at c.

questions.stem: Why was Compton scattering important evidence for the particle model of light?
options: The electrons were emitted only above a threshold frequency, whatever the X-ray intensity
The results matched a collision in which a photon carrying momentum h/λ conserved momentum and energy
The scattered X-rays formed an interference pattern, which only particles are able to produce
The X-rays were scattered without any change in wavelength, as the particle model predicts
questions.explanation: Treating each X-ray photon as a particle with momentum p = h/λ = E/c, and applying conservation of momentum and energy as in a collision, correctly predicted the wavelength change. Wave theory predicted no change in wavelength.

questions.stem: A 50.0 keV X-ray photon is Compton scattered by a stationary electron, and the scattered photon has an energy of 45.0 keV. What is the kinetic energy of the recoiling electron?
options: 95.0 keV
45.0 keV
50.0 keV
5.0 keV
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved: the electron gains what the photon loses, 50.0 − 45.0 = 5.0 keV. Momentum is also conserved, which fixes the directions in which the photon and electron move.

questions.stem: An X-ray photon of wavelength 2.00 × 10⁻¹¹ m is Compton scattered and leaves with wavelength 2.24 × 10⁻¹¹ m. What kinetic energy does the electron gain? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The incident photon has hc/λ = 9.95 × 10⁻¹⁵ J and the scattered one 8.88 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. The electron gains the difference, 1.07 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. Using hc/Δλ gives 8.29 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, which is not an energy anyone has.

questions.stem: In a Compton collision, an X-ray photon scatters straight back along its original path. Which statement about the recoiling electron is correct?
options: It moves forward with momentum larger than the incident photon's momentum
It moves backward with the scattered photon, sharing its momentum
It stays at rest, because the photon simply reverses its direction
It moves forward with momentum smaller than the incident photon's momentum
questions.explanation: Taking forward as positive, p(photon before) = p(electron) − p(photon after), so p(electron) = p₁ + p₂, larger than the incident photon's momentum. Like a ball bouncing off a wall, reversing the photon transfers the most momentum and gives the largest wavelength change.

questions.stem: The EM spectrum runs from radio waves to gamma rays. How does the behaviour of the radiation change along it?
options: Radio waves behave most like waves, and gamma rays behave most like particles
Radio waves behave most like particles, and gamma rays behave most like waves
All parts behave equally as waves and particles, whatever their energy
Only visible light shows both wave and particle behaviour in experiments
questions.explanation: As photon energy and momentum rise, particle behaviour such as collisions becomes easier to see, and as wavelength grows, wave effects such as diffraction dominate. X-rays and gamma rays show particle behaviour, as in Compton scattering.

questions.stem: Hydrogen atoms in the ground state (−13.6 eV) have a first excited level at −3.4 eV. They are bombarded first with 11.0 eV electrons, then with 11.0 eV photons. What happens?
options: The photons can excite the atoms, but the electrons pass through without any effect
Both the electrons and the photons can excite the atoms to the first excited level
Neither can excite the atoms, because 11.0 eV is less than the ionisation energy
The electrons can excite the atoms, but the photons pass through without being absorbed
questions.explanation: Exciting the atom needs exactly 10.2 eV. A colliding electron can give up 10.2 eV and keep the remaining 0.8 eV. A photon is absorbed only whole, so it must have exactly the energy of a transition; an 11.0 eV photon matches none.

questions.stem: A 15.0 eV photon is absorbed by a hydrogen atom in its ground state, whose ionisation energy is 13.6 eV. What happens?
options: The atom is ionised, and the freed electron has 1.4 eV of kinetic energy
The atom is excited to a higher level and later emits a 15.0 eV photon
The photon is not absorbed, because it does not match an energy level
The atom is ionised, and the freed electron has 15.0 eV of kinetic energy
questions.explanation: A photon with more energy than the ionisation energy can remove the electron completely, and the excess becomes the electron's kinetic energy: 15.0 − 13.6 = 1.4 eV. Above the ionisation energy, any photon energy can be absorbed.

questions.stem: Which methods can excite the atoms of a gas so that they emit a line spectrum?
options: Only compressing the gas, so that its atoms collide with the container walls
Heating the gas, passing an electric discharge through it, or shining suitable light on it
Only shining light on the gas, because only photons carry energy between atoms
Only cooling the gas, so that its electrons fall to lower energy levels
questions.explanation: Atoms can be raised to higher levels by collisions in a hot gas, by electron bombardment in a discharge tube, or by absorbing photons of the right energy. They then emit photons as electrons return to lower levels.
